definition: Inveterate means firmly fixed in a long-standing habit.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word inveterate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know inveterate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: An inveterate eavesdropper, Aunt Bettina chose café tables the way generals choose hills.
Recurring only says a thing comes back — it stops well short of inveterate, a habit grown into the person.
Ingrained habits run deep, yet even they stop short of inveterate, which has hardened over years past any real hope of reform.

Habitual is neutral bookkeeping: the thing is done by settled habit, and that is all it says -- a habitual jogger may have started last spring. Inveterate counts decades, not occurrences, and signals a habit fused into the person's identity, well past reforming.

Confirmed says a person has settled into a role and is unlikely to leave it -- a confirmed bachelor, a confirmed skeptic. It marks the state as fixed. Inveterate adds the long history behind that state: the decades of repetition that fused the habit into the person.

Inveterate means firmly fixed in a long-standing habit.
My grandfather haggles at the fixed-price supermarket, at the toll booth, and once — successfully — at a parking meter.
Sixty years of market stalls made him an inveterate bargainer, and no checkout screen will unmake him.
Inveterate is for habits that have grown into the person — in- ('into') + vetus ('old'): grown old in it.
It sits before the noun (an inveterate liar, an inveterate optimist) and resists reform by definition.
Frequent counts occurrences; inveterate counts decades.
Inveterate always modifies the doer (an inveterate punster) and always signals decades — habit fused into identity, past reforming.
Habitual is neutral bookkeeping; chronic belongs to conditions.
It usually smiles wryly: inveterate collectors are teased, not condemned.

Great-Aunt Philomena wrote letters the way other people breathe, and had done so since President Eisenhower's first term.
Three a day, minimum: to cousins, to editors, to the water board, once to an astronaut who wrote back.
Email arrived and was declined.
Arthritis arrived and was met with a thicker pen.
Nothing in seventy years so much as slowed the flow.
The family called her an inveterate correspondent, and meant it precisely: the writing was not a pastime she had kept up but a fixture of who she was, past all argument or reform.
When she died, the post office on Millbrook Lane observed a minute's silence, unasked.
